label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
**4 stars out of 5 — a real improvement for our livestream, with some limitations**

We bought the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 from Chancel AV in February 2026 for $2,140, plus $95 for the wall mount. **My rating is 4 stars out of 5.** I would buy it again for our situation, but I would not tell every small congregation that it needs to spend this much.

I write this as a pastor, not an engineer. We had been livestreaming worship with a webcam since 2020. Our nave is 92 feet long, and the PT-20 is mounted on the balcony rail at the back. It has a 20x optical zoom, 1080p60 video, NDI HX and a regular HDMI output. We use Power over Ethernet, so only one cable had to go up to the balcony.

The camera feeds OBS on our old office PC, and from there we stream to our YouTube channel. We usually have between 30 and 60 viewers on a Sunday. I cannot give a detailed technical comparison with other cameras, but the improvement over the webcam is obvious, particularly when we zoom in from the back of the church.

We have stored nine presets: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, wide, and two positions for the chancel steps. That has made the camera practical for volunteers. Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, operates it from the free web app on a tablet. He learned the system in one afternoon.

Setup did produce two problems. On our first Sunday, the presets drifted a few degrees by the time we reached the sermon. We installed firmware update 2.4 in March, and that fixed the drifting. The other issue is autofocus: it tends to hunt when someone walks between the camera and the pulpit. Our solution is to lock the focus on the presets. That works for us, but it is something another church should know about before buying.

Low-light performance is better than our old camera, though not miraculous. At our Easter Vigil in April, during the first “Christ the Lord Is Risen Today,” the church was lit only by candles. The picture became grainy, but it stayed usable. In similar conditions, our old webcam had shown little more than dots.

The most meaningful improvement came in a telephone call from Delores, who is 82 and homebound. She told us she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That matters more to us than any specification on the box.

The manual is thin and badly translated. On the other hand, Chancel AV’s technical support was very good. Marcy was excellent when we called, which made a considerable difference to people who do not install equipment like this every week.

One thing this camera did **not** fix was our sound problem. Audio is not its job. If your livestream is difficult to hear, buying a better camera will not change that; you will need to address the sound separately.

For us, the long nave, the zoom, and the easy use of presets have justified the purchase. But a congregation under 100, especially one worshiping in a smaller room, may do perfectly well with something less expensive. Do not assume that spending this much is necessary simply because you want a more dependable stream.

This camera greatly improved what our online congregation can see. It did not improve our audio, the manual needs work, and we had to deal with firmware and focus issues. That is why I give it four stars rather than five—and why, with those qualifications, I would buy it again.
